content: Cinnamon, scientifically known as Cinnamomum verum (synonym Cinnamomum zeylanicum), is a small evergreen tree that grows to a height of 10 to 15 meters (approximately 33 to 49 feet). It belongs to the Lauraceae family and is native to Sri Lanka and South India. The bark of this tree is highly valued as a spice due to its distinctive aroma. In India, it is commonly referred to as Daalchini. The leaves of the cinnamon tree are ovate-oblong in shape, measuring 7 to 18 cm (approximately 2.75 to 7.1 inches) in length. The flowers are arranged in panicles, exhibit a greenish hue, and emit a characteristic odor. The fruit is a small, purple berry, about one centimeter in size, containing a single seed. The unique flavor of cinnamon is attributed to its aromatic essential oil, which constitutes 0.5% to 1% of its composition. This oil is extracted by pounding the bark, soaking it in seawater, and then distilling it. The resulting oil is golden-yellow in color, possesses the characteristic cinnamon aroma, and has a hot, spicy taste. The pungency and scent of cinnamon are primarily due to cinnamaldehyde (cinnamic aldehyde). Over time, as the oil absorbs oxygen, it darkens in color and forms resinous compounds. The essential oil also contains other chemical components, including ethyl cinnamate, eugenol, beta-caryophyllene, linalool, and methyl chavicol. The term cinnamon is derived from the Greek word kinnámōmon, which has its origins in Phoenician and Hebrew (qinnâmôn). Ultimately, the name traces back to a Malaysian language, where it is referred to as kayu manis, meaning sweet wood. Historical Significance Cinnamon has been known since ancient times and was highly prized by various civilizations, often regarded as a gift suitable for royalty and other prominent figures. It was imported into Egypt from China as early as 2000 BCE. The Bible references cinnamon in Exodus 30:23, where Moses is instructed to use sweet cinnamon (qinnāmôn in Hebrew) and cassia, and in Proverbs 7:17-18, where it is mentioned as a perfume for a lover's bed. Classical writers, including Herodotus, also alluded to cinnamon. In ancient Rome, cinnamon was used in funeral rites, and Emperor Nero is said to have burned a year's supply of cinnamon at the funeral of his wife, Poppaea Sabina, in 65 CE. During the Middle Ages, the source of cinnamon was a mystery to Europeans. Arab traders transported the spice overland to Alexandria, Egypt, where Venetian merchants monopolized its trade in Europe. The rise of Mediterranean powers such as the Mamluk Sultans and the Ottoman Empire disrupted this trade, prompting Europeans to seek alternative routes to Asia. Portuguese traders discovered Ceylon (modern-day Sri Lanka) in the late 15th century and restructured cinnamon production, relying on the local Salagama caste. The Portuguese established a fort on the island in 1518 and maintained a monopoly for over a century. In 1638, Dutch traders allied with the inland Kingdom of Kandy in Ceylon to displace the Portuguese. By 1658, the Dutch had expelled the Portuguese entirely and took control of cinnamon production. A Dutch captain once remarked that the shores of Ceylon were so abundant with cinnamon that its aroma could be detected eight leagues out to sea. The Dutch East India Company refined harvesting methods and began cultivating cinnamon trees. However, by 1796, the British had taken control of Ceylon from the Dutch. By this time, the monopoly on Ceylon cinnamon had diminished in importance due to the spread of cinnamon cultivation to other regions, the increasing acceptance of cassia bark, and the growing popularity of other commodities such as coffee, tea, sugar, and chocolate. As of 2005, Indonesia was the largest producer of cinnamon, accounting for nearly 40% of global output, followed by China, India, and Vietnam. Cultivation Process Cinnamon is harvested by allowing the tree to grow for two years before coppicing it. The following year, multiple shoots sprout from the roots. These shoots are stripped of their bark, which is then left to dry. Only the thin inner bark, approximately 0.5 mm thick, is used. The outer woody layer is removed, leaving long strips of cinnamon bark that curl into quills as they dry. Each quill is composed of strips from multiple shoots packed together. These quills are then cut into smaller pieces, typically 5 to 10 cm in length, for sale. Cinnamon is primarily grown in Sri Lanka but is also cultivated commercially in regions such as Tellicherry in southern India, Java, Sumatra, the West Indies, Brazil, Vietnam, Madagascar, Zanzibar, and Egypt. Sri Lankan cinnamon is characterized by its thin, smooth bark, light yellowish-brown color, and highly fragrant aroma. Cinnamon vs. Cassia The term cinnamon is technically reserved for Ceylon cinnamon (Cinnamomum verum), also known as true cinnamon. However, related species such as cassia (Cinnamomum aromaticum) and Cinnamomum burmannii are often sold under the label of cinnamon. Cassia is sometimes referred to as Indonesian cinnamon or bastard cinnamon. True cinnamon, derived from the thin inner bark, has a finer, more crumbly texture and a milder flavor compared to cassia. Cassia bark is thicker (2-3 mm), harder, and more woody in texture, as it includes all layers of the bark. Most powdered cinnamon sold in U.S. supermarkets is actually cassia. True cinnamon is typically available in stick form in the U.S. European health agencies have cautioned against consuming large amounts of cassia due to its high coumarin content, a compound known to cause liver and kidney damage in high concentrations. Ceylon cinnamon and Cinnamomum burmannii contain much lower levels of coumarin. Whole cinnamon and cassia barks are easily distinguishable, and their microscopic characteristics are distinct. Cinnamon quills consist of multiple thin layers and can be ground into powder using a coffee or spice grinder, whereas cassia sticks are harder and can damage grinders. When powdered bark is treated with tincture of iodine (a test for starch), pure cinnamon shows little reaction, while cassia produces a deep blue coloration, the intensity of which depends on the proportion of cassia present. Culinary and Medicinal Uses Cinnamon bark is widely used as a spice and flavoring agent. It is commonly employed in desserts, chocolate, spicy candies, tea, hot cocoa, and liqueurs. In Middle Eastern cuisine, it is often used in savory dishes featuring chicken and lamb. In the United States, cinnamon is frequently combined with sugar to flavor cereals, bread-based dishes, and fruits, particularly apples. Pre-mixed cinnamon-sugar blends are also commercially available. Additionally, cinnamon is used in pickling. Cinnamon bark is one of the few spices that can be consumed directly. Medicinally, it has been used for its volatile oils, which were once believed to cure colds. It has also been employed to treat diarrhea and other digestive issues. Cinnamon exhibits high antioxidant activity and possesses antimicrobial properties, which contribute to its use in food preservation. While cinnamon has been reported to have potential benefits in managing type II diabetes, studies have often used cassia rather than true cinnamon. Traditionally, cinnamon has been used to alleviate toothache, combat bad breath, and support digestion. It is also believed to help prevent the common cold. In Thelemic Magick, cinnamon is associated with the invocation of Apollo, as described in Aleister Crowley's Liber 777. Additionally, cinnamon serves as a natural insect repellent.
